analysis.one_liner: Lets 50-to-64-year-olds buy into Medicare, adds a public supplemental plan, and repeals Medicaid work requirements.
analysis.headline: Introduced March 12, 2026 with a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors, the bill has sat without a hearing, markup, or vote in two House committees ever since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let uninsured or marketplace-covered adults aged 50 to 64 buy into Medicare at premiums set to cover the program's cost, with subsidies for lower-income enrollees. It would also create a government-run supplemental plan covering Medicare deductibles and copays, require the Health Secretary to negotiate Medicare drug prices with manufacturers, repeal the health provisions of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act including Medicaid work requirements, and restore generous premium tax credits for marketplace plans. It has not moved past its committee referrals.
analysis.who_benefits: Adults aged 50 to 64 without Medicare coverage — a group that includes many early retirees and workers whose employers dropped or never offered coverage — could buy into Medicare with financial help modeled on Affordable Care Act subsidies. Current Medicare beneficiaries would gain a public plan covering their deductibles and copays and lower drug prices through government negotiation. Marketplace enrollees above 400% of the poverty line would get premium tax credits restored for them, and adults on the Medicaid expansion would no longer have to meet work or community-service requirements to keep coverage.

how_it_helps.text: Allows anyone aged 50 to 64 who would qualify for Medicare at 65 to enroll immediately in the same Part A, B, and D benefits, including Medicare Advantage plans, with premiums set by formula and subsidies similar to ACA premium tax credits and cost-sharing reductions for lower-income enrollees.

Creates a voluntary public supplemental option that pays Medicare deductibles, copays, and other cost-sharing after a $100 annual deductible, with community-rated premiums, a 10%-per-year late-enrollment penalty, and no pre-existing-condition exclusions.

Strikes the current 'noninterference' rule and requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate prices, discounts, and rebates for covered Part D drugs with manufacturers, effective for plan years beginning January 1, 2029.

Repeals the health subtitle of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (Public Law 119-21), including its requirement that Medicaid expansion adults meet work or community-engagement requirements to keep coverage.
Removes the 400%-of-poverty income cap on premium tax credits and lowers the share of income families must pay for premiums, effective for tax years after 2026.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug makers would take lower negotiated prices on Medicare Part D drugs. Medigap and other private supplemental insurers would face direct competition from a public plan with community-rated premiums and no underwriting. Marketplace health plans would pay fees into a new reinsurance fund, and insurers generally would lose some customers to the Medicare buy-in and public supplemental option. Federal spending would rise through expanded premium tax credits, buy-in subsidies, and $500 million per year in outreach and enrollment grants from 2026 through 2028.
analysis.who_pays_short: Drug makers, Medigap insurers, federal taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Buy-in premiums are set at the estimated full per-person cost of Parts A, B, and D, and the Secretary must adjust them so Medicare spending does not increase because of the program — so monthly premiums for 50-to-64-year-olds could still be substantial, especially for those above the subsidy thresholds.
Expanding premium tax credits without an income cap and running $500 million per year in outreach grants adds new federal spending with no offset specified in the bill text.

The new reinsurance fund pays insurers 80% of individual-market claims above roughly $50,000 up to a cap, financed by fees on marketplace plans — a subsidy to insurers that could partly flow back into premiums.

Because older and sicker enrollees would have the most reason to join the buy-in, the bill lets the Secretary charge separate premiums by age specifically to reduce the risk of adverse selection, an admission that the risk pool could otherwise become unbalanced.
Repealing the health subtitle of Public Law 119-21 would unwind enacted law wholesale, including provisions beyond the work requirement, a large policy and budget reversal made in a single provision.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households in the target groups, the benefits are direct and concrete: a Medicare option before 65, out-of-pocket cost coverage, lower drug prices, and richer marketplace subsidies. The costs are mostly shifted onto drug manufacturers, supplemental insurers, and the federal budget, and the bill offers no offsets for its new spending. Its weakest point is the buy-in premium design: because premiums must be self-financing, a 55-year-old could still face a bill of several hundred dollars a month, which limits how much relief the headline benefit delivers in practice.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees the day it was introduced and has had no hearing, markup, or vote since.

narrative.text: Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi introduced H.R. 7909, the Medicare Expansion and Lowering Costs Now Act, in the House on March 12, 2026.
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and, in addition, to the Committee on Ways and Means, with the Speaker to decide how the jurisdiction is divided.
No other members have cosponsored the bill, which lists zero cosponsors on Congress.gov.
The full action history shows no further steps after the committee referrals — no hearings, markups, or votes are recorded.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing has changed yet, so the industries the bill would charge or displace — drug makers and private supplemental insurers — keep current law, while the near-retirees, Medicare beneficiaries, and Medicaid expansion adults it would help have gained nothing so far.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has one Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors, and it sits without action in two committees whose chairs are Republicans; no votes have occurred, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.note: The bill repeals the statutory 'noninterference' rule and requires the Health Secretary to negotiate Part D drug prices with manufacturers starting in 2029. Negotiated prices cut what beneficiaries and the government pay for prescriptions, which is exactly the revenue these companies would give up.

A new government-run supplemental option would cover Medicare deductibles and copays with community-rated premiums, a $100 deductible, and no pre-existing-condition screening, competing directly with Medigap policies. The bill also requires Medigap issuers to guarantee issue to buy-in enrollees during set windows.

industries.industry: Health insurers (Medicare Advantage and marketplace plans)
industries.note: The bill cuts both ways for insurers: buy-in enrollees may enroll in Medicare Advantage plans, giving insurers new customers, and a new reinsurance fund pays them 80% of high-cost individual-market claims. But marketplace plans pay fees to fund that reinsurance, and the public supplemental option and buy-in would pull some customers out of private coverage.

Licensed agents and brokers arranged with states or nonprofits are eligible for outreach and enrollment grants funded at $500 million per year through 2028, though entities taking money from health insurers are excluded.

analysis.trajectory: With a single sponsor, zero cosponsors, and a dual referral to two committees run by the opposing party, this bill is very unlikely to get a hearing or a floor vote before this Congress ends in January 2027. It would need to pick up cosponsors quickly and receive a leadership decision to move; absent that, the realistic path is that it expires in committee at the end of the session.
